query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled induction of grain boundary serrations in an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating enhances its creep resistance by mitigating localized dislocation creep and distributing plastic strain more uniformly under sustained loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy-alloy protective coating with predominantly straight grain boundaries that, under continuous loading, exhibits progressive plastic deformation governed by dislocation creep.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored thermal treatment to modify the coating’s microstructure, promoting the development of serrated grain boundaries without altering its overall composition.
generation.conditions: Sustained high-temperature (around 650°C) and continuous mechanical loading, representing the operational environment where plastic deformation is observed.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary morphology; specifically, serrated boundaries that can disperse local strain concentrations compared to straight boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The serrated grain boundaries interfere with the motion of dislocations by diffusing local strain concentrations, thereby hindering the progression of dislocation creep and delaying intergranular crack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline coating with straight grain boundaries, the treated coating with serrated boundaries will show a reduced creep strain rate, increased time-to-failure, and more uniform strain distribution under identical high-temperature loading conditions.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy-alloy coating with straight grain boundaries that exhibits notable dislocation creep and accelerated plastic deformation under continuous loading.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under sustained high-temperature conditions (e.g., around 650°C) and within the tested mechanical loading regimes (e.g., similar to loading conditions observed at 2.5 mN/s in related studies), while maintaining similar alloy compositions and microstructural phases (FCC/BCC).
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which other factors (such as variations in elemental content like Al, or precipitate formation) might interact with grain boundary morphology to affect creep resistance remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings with identical compositions: one set processed to retain straight grain boundaries (control) and the other processed using a modified thermal treatment to induce grain boundary serrations. Subject both sets to sustained high-temperature (≈650°C) and continuous mechanical loading conditions.
measurements: Grain boundary morphology characterization using microscopy
Local strain distribution via digital image correlation or similar techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the serrated-boundary coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate and an increase in time-to-failure with more uniform strain distribution than the control coatings, then the hypothesis that grain boundary serrations improve creep resistance is falsified.

AbstractHigh-temperature creep refers to the slow and continuous plastic deformation of materials under the effects of high temperatures and mechanical stress over extended periods, which can lead to the degradation or even failure of the components’ functionality. AlxCr0.2NbTiV (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8) refractory high-entropy alloys were fabricated by arc melting. The effects of Al content on the microstructure of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were studied using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction. The microhardness, compression properties, and nanoindentation creep properties of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were also tested. The results show that the AlxCr0.2NbTiV series exhibits a BCC single-phase structure. As the Al content increases, the lattice constant of the alloys gradually decreases, and the intensity of the (110) crystal plane diffraction peak increases. Adding aluminum enhances the effect of solution strengthening; however, due to grain coarsening, the microhardness and room temperature compressive strength of the alloy are only slightly improved. ## Abstract
ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
